Viewed Most of the engineers I talk to are waiting for something.

For their company to send them on a Kubernetes course.
For a manager to notice they've outgrown the role.
For a hiring market that feels less uncertain.
For the AI situation to settle down so they know what's worth learning.

I understand the instinct. But none of those things arrive on a schedule you control.

One of my students, Alba, didn't wait. She saw a gap in her company that nobody was covering, put together a case for why the role should exist, and pitched it internally.

She wasn't the most senior person in the room. She was the one who showed up with a proposal instead of a request. (side note: will share more about how she broke into DevOps in a few weeks😊)

That pattern shows up in almost every student who ends up somewhere they're happy with. Not the most talented ones. The ones who moved first.

On September 13th I'm running a free three-hour live session on what's actually changed in DevOps hiring, and which skills still hold up now that AI has taken over a chunk of the routine work.

Live only. Be sure to sign up - seats are capped: https://bit.ly/4iMBvoX

Viewed A man drove around 1,700 miles from Cornwall to the Isle of Lewis just to make 52 calls from a remote phone box and help keep its line connected.

William Arnold spent nearly two hours making the calls and got through around £36 in coins, because 52 calls in 12 months is one of the Ofcom criteria that can protect a qualifying phone box from being removed.

The box itself is pretty special too. It's an incredibly rare double-door K6, designed for the brutal Hebridean weather, and is believed to be the last connected example of its kind still in its original location.

William has been documenting Britain's disappearing phone boxes for years, so as ridiculous as the mission sounds, there is actually a serious point behind it.

1,700 miles and £36 in change to save a red phone box.
Incredible commitment to the cause

Viewed Goodbye my friend. Over the years one friendship kept growing that I never expected… but every time I traveled there was always one person there:

Farooq Ahmad. 

Farooq, you were one of the kindest and most honorable men I’ve met. Your positivity and upbeat energy always uplifted me and made our trips better. Whether we were filming, flying, or taking an Uber with 4 hours of sleep, you made each moment fun and unforgettable.

I respected Farooq’s deep commitment to his values and faith, and from my time with him I knew he always upheld them even when no one was looking. He left an indelible mark on our community, and his absence will be felt for a very, very long time.

I can’t fully put into words the shock and sadness I feel today. Just weeks ago we were flying across the country, meeting Tom Holland, and the two of us sat down for a late dinner after working for 5 straight days. We talked about PUBG MOBILE, but over the years our conversations broadened. As we got to know each other we discussed life, family, and the world.

I will greatly miss our conversations and seeing you every few months on our adventures. So many of my fondest memories include Farooq. From movie premieres and driving race cars, to amazing meals and funny vlogs, he will always be a part of my best moments as a creator.

Farooq was a true friend and finding someone of his caliber is rare.

Rest in peace, Farooq.

The full MoTeC package for the C6 Z06 just landed:

M150 ECU - full standalone engine management. Advanced traction control, drive-by-wire strategies, GPS-based DRS deployment and a lot more.

C1812 colour display logger - dash and data logger in one. Every lap, every sensor, every corner recorded and analysed properly instead of guessing or driver excuses. After driving the Cup car, I fell in love with big screen and wanted one for my Corvette. But the C1812 is REALLY BIG (maybe I can connect my Netflix to it?) and it looks like we need to fabricate our own dashboard for it. Oh noooooo. While we're at it, might as well🤣

2x PDM30 - no fuse box, no relays. Solid-state power distribution with programmable current limits, remote diagnostics and a fraction of the wiring weight.

4x LTCD dual lambda modules - 8 channels of wideband, one per cylinder.

CAN keypad, GPS, camera - everything on one network, everything logged, everything visible.

Overkill? Not at all once you see our plans with this build. This is also something for NEXT SEASON, as custom wiring and calibration by ECU Plus will take a lot of time. And we are already working on next year's iteration of the car. It's going to be mental😈

Among those who gathered was Caroline Mutisya, whose son, Erickson Kyalo Mutisya, was killed near Parliament during the protests.

"I came here today to remember my son, who was killed just 50 metres from Parliament, and to demand justice for his death," she told the BBC.

Viewed Your environment shapes how you work. More than most people realize.

I finally made some real changes to my office last month — added plants (okay, maybe overdid it a little 🌿😁), adjusted the lighting, made the whole space feel less like a room you sit in and more like a place you actually want to be in.

And it made a difference. Immediately.

When you're doing deep work — really sitting down to think through a complex topic, write, research, build something — the space around you is not neutral. It either supports that state or it fights it. There's no in-between.

For me that looks like: good lighting, plants around me, no clutter, and a setup that signals to my brain "this is where we create." The morning ritual with coffee before the laptop even opens helps too.

It sounds small. But these things compound.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁'𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗺𝗮𝗱𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝗰𝘂𝘀?

------------

This week we also reached out to some of our most committed graduates to share their engineering journeys. Many don't even realize how much their path can help someone else who is at the exact same starting point — what worked, what didn't, how they navigated upskilling while still working full-time etc. 

And you can't imagine how diverse these paths are: 
- a software engineer who used her maternity leave to upskill, 
- an IT student who went through every single TWN program while doing his apprenticeship and landed a permanent role, 
- and a cybersecurity SME with 30 years of experience who decided to cross into DevSecOps. 

Some already agreed - so excited to share soon 🙂

------------

And while I was deep in all of this, one message caught my attention.

Feedback came in from one of our students, who just started his journey. He spent the last 10 years in HR as a Technical Recruiter hiring for engineering roles.

So he spent years hiring for technical roles, gained deep insight into what companies look for in strong engineers, and watched the hiring trends evolve up close. Nobody understands the market better than someone who lived on that side of the table.

At some point he decided he didn't just want to recruit engineers anymore. He wanted to become one 💪

And with everything he knows about the industry — he chose DevOps and Cloud as his path:
"𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐏𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝟏, 𝐈 𝐝𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐟𝐮𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐢𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐟𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐍𝐚𝐧𝐚’𝐬 𝟔-𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡 𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐭, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐢𝐭 𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐝 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐟𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐥𝐲 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐦𝐞."

He printed all the materials, spiral-bound them into books, built his own study guide — and just follows the structure without overthinking it.

Love seeing students with such commitment, because I know - no matter what obstacles - they will always succeed 💙

Have a great Sunday and productive week ahead! 🙏

Viewed My embarrassing failures before I became a tech educator 👀 - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aQxPcWq2QxM
.
Most people know me as "that confident tech educator" with clear explanations and millions of views. My comments are filled with words like "naturally talented" and (cringe) "genius"...

But here's the truth that might shock you:

I failed a basic English test that had questions like "He __ to school" (go/goes/going/gone). Yes, seriously 🙉

I was also probably the first student in history to fail writing "Hello World" TWICE in a row. My professor gave me a ZERO... TWICE!

I even failed the simplest SQL query exam (just basic SELECT statements) that every other student passed easily 🥹

Yet today? I teach complex engineering concepts to millions of developers... in English!

How does someone go from these spectacular failures to becoming successful in the exact same areas they initially failed at? 🤷‍♀️

That's what I'm sharing in this video, as my full journey and the pattern I discovered behind nearly EVERY successful person you may admire (including Abraham Lincoln, Michael Jordan and others who faced massive early rejections).

The most valuable part comes at the end - a simple 30-day challenge that completely transforms how you view failure ✅

This isn't about "never giving up" or motivational talk - it's much more practical than that..

Let me know what resonates the most in the video 👇

Here's why 👇

😍 "𝑰 𝒓𝒆𝒂𝒍𝒊𝒛𝒆𝒅 𝑰 𝒄𝒐𝒖𝒍𝒅 𝒉𝒂𝒗𝒆 𝒏𝒆𝒗𝒆𝒓 𝒓𝒆𝒂𝒄𝒉𝒆𝒅 𝒕𝒉𝒊𝒔 𝒍𝒆𝒗𝒆𝒍 𝒐𝒇 𝒌𝒏𝒐𝒘𝒍𝒆𝒅𝒈𝒆 𝒃𝒚 𝒅𝒐𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝒔𝒆𝒑𝒂𝒓𝒂𝒕𝒆 𝒄𝒐𝒖𝒓𝒔𝒆𝒔 𝒐𝒇 𝒆𝒂𝒄𝒉 𝒕𝒐𝒐𝒍 𝒂𝒏𝒅 𝒂𝒑𝒑𝒓𝒆𝒄𝒊𝒂𝒕𝒆 𝒃𝒆𝒕𝒕𝒆𝒓 𝒂𝒍𝒍 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒆𝒇𝒇𝒐𝒓𝒕 𝒊𝒕 𝒕𝒂𝒌𝒆𝒔 𝒕𝒐 𝒑𝒖𝒕 𝒂𝒏𝒅 𝒎𝒂𝒊𝒏𝒕𝒂𝒊𝒏 𝒂𝒍𝒍 𝒕𝒉𝒊𝒔 𝒕𝒐𝒈𝒆𝒕𝒉𝒆𝒓."

- Got this from Francisco, an experienced systems admin who's done plenty of training over the years.

And on the SAME day I got this feedback from someone who's considering our DevOps program:

🥺 "𝑰'𝒎 𝒏𝒐𝒕 𝒔𝒖𝒓𝒆 𝒉𝒐𝒘 𝒚𝒐𝒖𝒓 𝒃𝒐𝒐𝒕𝒄𝒂𝒎𝒑 𝒘𝒐𝒖𝒍𝒅 𝒉𝒆𝒍𝒑 𝒎𝒆 𝒍𝒂𝒏𝒅 𝒂 𝒋𝒐𝒃. 𝑰𝒕 𝒍𝒐𝒐𝒌𝒔 𝒍𝒊𝒌𝒆 𝒂 𝒄𝒐𝒍𝒍𝒆𝒄𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏 𝒐𝒇 𝒕𝒆𝒄𝒉𝒏𝒊𝒄𝒂𝒍 𝒄𝒐𝒖𝒓𝒔𝒆𝒔 𝑰 𝒄𝒐𝒖𝒍𝒅 𝒇𝒊𝒏𝒅 𝒄𝒉𝒆𝒂𝒑𝒆𝒓 𝒆𝒍𝒔𝒆𝒘𝒉𝒆𝒓𝒆. 𝑰 𝒘𝒐𝒖𝒍𝒅 𝒆𝒙𝒑𝒆𝒄𝒕 𝒎𝒐𝒓𝒆 𝒇𝒐𝒄𝒖𝒔 𝒐𝒏 𝒋𝒐𝒃-𝒓𝒆𝒂𝒅𝒊𝒏𝒆𝒔𝒔 𝒂𝒔𝒑𝒆𝒄𝒕𝒔 𝒔𝒖𝒄𝒉 𝒂𝒔 𝒉𝒐𝒘 𝒕𝒐 𝒊𝒎𝒑𝒓𝒐𝒗𝒆 𝒑𝒆𝒓𝒔𝒐𝒏𝒂𝒍 𝒃𝒓𝒂𝒏𝒅𝒊𝒏𝒈, 𝒕𝒂𝒊𝒍𝒐𝒓 𝒂 𝑪𝑽."

I'm happy to get such honest feedback.

Seriously, I'm not being sarcastic.

This is extremely valuable as a business owner.

Because it shows me the disconnect between what people expect and what our students actually experience.

Francisco - our graduate - continues:
"𝑰'𝒗𝒆 𝒓𝒆𝒂𝒍𝒍𝒚 𝒆𝒏𝒋𝒐𝒚𝒆𝒅 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒄𝒍𝒆𝒗𝒆𝒓 𝒘𝒂𝒚 𝒐𝒇 𝒃𝒖𝒊𝒍𝒅𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒄𝒐𝒏𝒏𝒆𝒄𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏𝒔 𝒃𝒆𝒕𝒘𝒆𝒆𝒏 𝒂𝒍𝒍 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒅𝒊𝒇𝒇𝒆𝒓𝒆𝒏𝒕 𝒕𝒐𝒐𝒍𝒔 𝒎𝒐𝒅𝒖𝒍𝒆 𝒂𝒇𝒕𝒆𝒓 𝒎𝒐𝒅𝒖𝒍𝒆 𝒔𝒐 𝒂𝒕 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒆𝒏𝒅 𝒚𝒐𝒖 𝒓𝒆𝒂𝒍𝒍𝒚 𝒈𝒆𝒕 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒃𝒊𝒈 𝒑𝒊𝒄𝒕𝒖𝒓𝒆 𝒏𝒆𝒆𝒅𝒆𝒅 𝒊𝒏 𝒕𝒉𝒊𝒔 𝒇𝒊𝒆𝒍𝒅."

So from the outside, yeah - it probably does look like "just another bundle of courses."

But that's not what it is.

And I realized - if people are thinking this way, I need to explain it better.

Most platforms teach you Docker. Then Kubernetes. Then Jenkins. All separate.

Then you're supposed to figure out yourself how they fit together in a real job.

That's where people get stuck.

That's why I intentionally didn't built our program that way.

And about the career tips?

We actually added that last year. Weekly job prep tips, LinkedIn advice, tips on personal brand building, career advice throughout the learning journey. Again bad job in communication. 🙈

Even though honestly?

With AI now, you can create a personalized CV and motivation letter in minutes tailored to any job description. You have a personalized hiring expert at your finger tips.

But we added it anyway.

But let me be real: A great CV might get you the interview.

Understanding how to architect a CI/CD pipeline for their specific use case? That gets you the job 👉 https://bit.ly/students-voices

All of them will be on our Youtube channel soon 😃

These are actual journeys and results from our students.

Career switches. Senior positions. Multiple offers.

Soon, Isreal will be on camera.

Came from Nigeria to UK. Got 2 offers. Accepted a LEAD DevOps Engineer role.

That's why we started bringing people in front of the camera this year.

So you can hear from them what actually made the difference. And you can copy the path and apply it to your career.

Viewed Ghanaians are mourning the passing of former First Lady Nana Konadu Agyeman-Rawlings, who died on Thursday at the age of 76.⁣
⁣
She was the widow of Ghana’s longest-serving leader, Jerry John Rawlings, who died five years ago. As first lady, she founded the 31st December Women’s Movement to empower women and help them earn an income to develop their communities.⁣
⁣
Her advocacy shaped national policy - influencing a 1989 law guaranteeing inheritance rights for women and children - and contributed to gender equality provisions in Ghana’s 1992 constitution, which restored multi-party democracy.⁣
⁣

Viewed Kenyan innovator Elly Savatia has won the 2025 Africa Prize for Engineering Innovation for his sign language translation app, Terp 360.⁣
⁣
Awarded by the Royal Academy of Engineering, the £50,000 prize was announced at a live final in Dakar, Senegal, the first time the event has been hosted in Francophone Africa.⁣
⁣
Terp 360 uses AI to translate speech into sign language through 3D avatars, addressing interpreter shortages and improving accessibility in classrooms, workplaces, and public services.⁣
⁣
Three other finalists each received £10,000, with a £5,000 One to Watch prize also awarded.⁣
⁣
Launched in 2014, the Prize is Africa’s largest award for engineering innovation, providing funding, mentorship, and training to help entrepreneurs scale their solutions. ⁣

Viewed Members of a self-styled “African tribe” calling themselves the Kingdom of Kubala have been evicted from council-owned woodland in the Scottish Borders.
 
A convoy of police, sheriff’s officers and immigration officials moved in on Thursday morning, with the eviction streamed live on TikTok by the tribe. Drone footage showed dozens of uniformed officers entering the camp before detaining two members on suspicion of immigration offences.
 
The group - led by Ghanaian-born Kofi Offeh, who calls himself King Atehene, and his followers - claim they were reclaiming land stolen from their ancestors 400 years ago, and had refused to recognise the authority of the courts.
